## What stands out

- **Both benchmarks peak on the same day.** `brent-daily` and `wti-daily` both hit their maximum on 2008-07-03 (Brent $143.95, WTI $145.31) — the run-up just before the 2008 financial crisis.
- **WTI's daily minimum is the widely reported negative-price day.** -$36.98 on 2020-04-20. EIA attributes it to the expiring May futures contract and scarce storage at Cushing ([Today in Energy, 27 Apr 2020](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=43495)); the price data itself shows only that it happened. It is a one-day anomaly, not a sustained dip: 2020-04-17 was $18.31 and 2020-04-21 was $8.91. It also disappears once averaged — `wti-weekly` (min $3.32), `wti-monthly` ($11.35) and `wti-year` ($14.42) never go negative.
- **Brent's daily minimum is $9.10 on 1998-12-10** — the 1998 oil-glut low. Outside the 2020 anomaly, WTI's low across weekly/monthly/annual ($3.32/$11.35/$14.42) sits in a similar range to Brent's.
- **Brent trades at a slight premium on average** (mean ≈$51.4–51.5 across frequencies vs WTI's ≈$48.1–48.7), even though WTI briefly traded *above* Brent at their shared 2008 peak — consistent with the Brent–WTI spread that became persistent after 2010–11.
- **No missing values anywhere.** All eight series report `missing = 0`; EIA's spot-price data has no gaps to note.

## Trial notes

Friction and decisions from running `enrich` on a second dataset (co2-ppm was the first hand pass); for resolving the open questions in `skills/enrich/SKILL.md`.

- **Parallel resources — resolved by consolidation.** co2-ppm's draft left "collapse to one table with a resource column?" open. For eight same-schema resources sharing one measurement name (`Price`), a single consolidated table (one row per resource + measurement) is far more readable than eight near-identical one-row tables. Recommend the skill make this the default once more than one resource shares a measurement name.
- **Empty-population handling needed to be added.** co2-ppm never hit an all-missing column in practice, so its `numericStats` never had to decide what to do with `n = 0`. oil-prices has no such column either, but the acceptance bar required handling it: this `enrich.ts` returns `null` for min/max/mean/median/std dev when `n = 0`, rendered as a blank table cell rather than `NaN` or `0`. Worth folding into the skill as an explicit rule, not left implicit per-dataset.
- **Denominator convention should be stated, not just implemented.** Both enrich.ts scripts use population variance (denominator `n`). co2-ppm's SUMMARY.md never says so. This one states it in the table caption; the skill should require that.
- **Zero and negative values are easy to accidentally filter as "missing."** Confirmed the implementation only treats the empty string as missing — 2020-04-20's -$36.98 survives into the table. Worth a one-line test-writing reminder in the skill: a naive `Number(v) || undefined`-style guard would silently drop zero.
- **A stale/misleading view was caught along the way, not by the skill.** The pre-enrich `datapackage.json` had one view titled "Brent vs WTI spot price, daily" pointing at only `brent-daily` — a placeholder that promised a two-series comparison it didn't deliver. Fixed by splitting into two single-series views (`brent-daily`, `wti-daily`). Possibly worth a skill checklist item: "does every view's title match what its `resources`/`series` actually plot?"
